processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: 50 kg ingots of steel prepared by induction melting under an argon atmosphere
Homogenization at the same temperature (1200 °C) for 3 h prior to hot rolling
Hot rolled to a thickness of 3.5 mm with a reduction of 90%
Hot-rolled strips were annealed at 1000 °C for 1 h
Cold rolled to a thickness of 1 mm
Cold rolled strips were annealed at 1000 °C
Final anneal followed by water quenching to room temperature, giving the as-quenched state

structures.overall_structure: Duplex ferritic–austenitic microstructure (complex low density steel) in the as-quenched condition; austenite fraction 84.8%. Ordered phases exist in both phases: CsCl-type B2 [(Fe,Mn)Al] domains with fine Fm3m-type DO3 [(Fe,Mn)3Al] particles in ferrite, and L'12 (perovskite) type κ [(Fe,Mn)3AlCx] carbide in austenite. The 0.8C steel appears markedly finer/more mottled and weakly banded compared with 0.5C.

precipitates.distribution: fine DO3 particles within B2 domains in ferrite

structures.overall_structure: Microstructural evolution of 0.8C steel during tensile deformation (interrupted tensile tests combined with TEM): at true strain ε=0.01 planar slip traces in austenite and paired superdislocations in ferrite; at ε=0.18 microbands formed in austenite and the dislocation density in ferrite distinctly increased (dense dislocation tangles/cell walls). This underpins the two-stage strain hardening of the 0.8C steel.

defects.type: dense dislocation tangles / strongly increased dislocation density

defect_interactions.interaction_type: strain partitioning between ferrite and austenite affected by ordered phases
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: The strengthened ferrite phase resulting from the existence of the ordered phases may affect the strain partition between ferrite and austenite in the investigated 0.8C steel, causing the increasing trend in strain hardening as deformation proceeds (second stage stronger and extended to higher strains than 0.5C).

interfaces.slip_behavior: At ε=0.01 planar slip traces (dominant single slip) in austenite and paired superdislocations in ferrite; the presence of the ordered phase makes dislocation multiplication difficult. At ε=0.18 microbands form in austenite and dislocation density strongly increases in ferrite. No microband–microband interaction observed (limited plastic deformation capability), consistent with a two-stage hardening behaviour.
interfaces.phase_evolution: Two-stage strain hardening; first stage slope slightly steeper than 0.5C (attributed to κ carbides in austenite); second stage stronger and extended to higher strains than 0.5C due to ordered-phase-strengthened ferrite.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: constant crosshead displacement velocity; universal testing machine SANSCMT5000

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress–strain curve of the 0.8C steel (red curve in Fig. 3); plateau maximum just below 1000 MPa with abrupt load drop at a strain just under 0.4
strain_hardening_rate: two-stage strain hardening; C–J analysis breakpoint at ε=0.022

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: The 0.8C steel (UTS 979 MPa, elongation 38.4%, UTS×TE 37597 MPa·%) is superior to the Fe–20Mn–10Al–1.2C steel reported in Ref. [7] (881 MPa and 38.1%), and comparable to the as-quenched Fe–27Mn–12Al–0.8C steel [10] (995 MPa and 42%); specific strength 142.3 MPa·cm3/g

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: specimens prepared by standard mechanical polishing and etching with a solution of 1 ml hydrochloric acid, 100 ml methanol and 4 g picric acid
characterization_methods.purpose: Observe the as-quenched microstructure of the 0.8C steel (revealing the duplex ferritic–austenitic structure)
characterization_methods.key_findings: 0.8C steel has a finer, more mottled/equiaxed duplex ferritic–austenitic structure with weaker banding than the 0.5C steel

characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the volume fractions of different phases
characterization_methods.key_findings: Austenite volume fraction of the 0.8C steel determined to be 84.8%

characterization_methods.technique: transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with selected-area diffraction (SADP)
characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Tecnai G2 20 TEM at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV; thin foils prepared by twinjet electropolishing using 9% perchloric acid in methanol at −30 °C
characterization_methods.purpose: Detailed microstructural analysis of the as-quenched phases and precipitates; analysis of microstructural evolution during deformation (interrupted tensile tests)
characterization_methods.key_findings: 0.8C steel contains a κ carbide phase [(Fe,Mn)3AlCx] in austenite and B2 domains with fine DO3 particles in ferrite; twins observed in γ; during deformation planar slip at ε=0.01 and microbands plus increased dislocation density in ferrite at ε=0.18

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: room temperature; constant crosshead displacement velocity equivalent to an initial strain rate of 1.33×10^-3 s^-1
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the tensile properties (YS, UTS, TE) and obtain engineering stress–strain curves of the steels
characterization_methods.key_findings: 0.8C steel: YS 711.2 MPa, UTS 979.1 MPa, TE 38.4%, UTS×TE 37597 MPa·%

characterization_methods.technique: Crussard–Jaoul (C–J) differential strain-hardening analysis (ln(dσ/dε) vs lnε)
characterization_methods.purpose: Analyze the strain hardening behavior of the 0.8C steel and correlate stages with microstructural evolution
characterization_methods.key_findings: 0.8C steel exhibits a two-stage strain hardening with a breakpoint at ε=0.022

analytical_models.equation_role: calculates the density of the steels from composition [ref. 7]
analytical_models.model_note: Densities of the three steels were calculated as 6.92, 6.88 and 6.78 g/cm3 respectively; 0.8C steel = 6.88 g/cm3

analytical_models.equation_role: calculates austenite SFE using the model used previously [13]
analytical_models.model_note: SFE values of austenite in 0.5C and 0.8C steels are 73.4 and 77.9 mJ/m2 respectively

computational_details.validation_against_experiment: The C–J staging was validated against TEM microstructural changes during interrupted tensile tests

analytical_models.equation_role: ln(dσ/dε) vs lnε used to describe multi-stage strain hardening behavior
analytical_models.model_note: 0.5C and 0.8C steels exhibit a two-stage strain hardening by C–J analysis; the modified C–J analysis was also conducted for the 0.8C steel but no obvious descending was found

unmapped_findings: Measured chemical composition of the 0.8C steel (mass%): Al 9.91, Mn 17.14, C 0.77, Fe Bal. (Table 1).
Calculated density of the 0.8C steel is 6.88 g/cm3 (b0016).
Stacking fault energy (SFE) of austenite in the 0.8C steel is 77.9 mJ/m2, calculated with a previously used model [13] (b0016).
Specific strength of the 0.8C steel is 142.3 MPa·cm3/g (b0041).
Product of strength and elongation (UTS × TE) of the 0.8C steel is 37597 MPa·% (Table 2, Fig. 4, b0041).
The 0.8C steel is referred to as a 'complex low density steel' because both ferrite (B2 + fine DO3 particles) and austenite (κ carbide) contain ordered phases (b0020, b0033).
The 0.8C steel has a much smaller grain size than the 1.2C steel (qualitative, b0040).

The presence of the ordered phase makes dislocation multiplication difficult, resulting in dominant single slip in austenite of the 0.8C steel at low strain, in contrast to multi-slip in 0.5C steel (b0049).
